content:
Right now, to state that u ∘ v = id, we have two (definitionally equal) spellings: LeftInverse u v and RightInverse v u.

@Oliver Nash suggested to me that this is a bit weird: these are really the same notion with a different order of arguments, and the order of the arguments is not that intuitive.

What would people think of introducing Function.SemiInverse u v to mean u ∘ v = id? This would allow for deduplication of the API, and the order of arguments is clear (the left inverse is on the left, the right inverse is on the right).
(I'm open to better naming suggestions)
I am almost sure this has already been discussed, but good luck in finding the conversation...

I'm not really sure what to do here because it's one of those situations where we want to have a balance between useful API and minimising surprise relative to prevailing terminology in informal literature.

For me the name SemiInverse is a step too far. I'd probably just nuke RightInverse and add a comment to the doc string of Left.Inverse explaining why we don't have RightInverse.

It wasn't difficult :)
#mathlib4 > LeftInverse and RightInverse

Riccardo Brasca said:

It wasn't difficult :)
#mathlib4 > LeftInverse and RightInverse

Yes, I should have looked

Oliver Nash said:

For me the name SemiInverse is a step too far. I'd probably just nuke RightInverse and add a comment to the doc string of Left.Inverse explaining why we don't have RightInverse.

But the symmetry :tear:
gt wants to have a word about the symmetry argument.
Fair.
HasLeftInverse and HasRightInverse are not symmetrical in this way I note.
Maybe just call it Function.CompEqId. Similar names like LinearMap.injective_of_comp_eq_id, LinearMap.ker_eq_range_of_comp_eq_id and LinearMap.comp_eq_id_comm are already in use.
Personally, I quite like Function.SemiInverse

Anatole Dedecker said:

Oliver Nash said:

For me the name SemiInverse is a step too far. I'd probably just nuke RightInverse and add a comment to the doc string of Left.Inverse explaining why we don't have RightInverse.

But the symmetry :tear:

I think SectionRetraction (instead of RightInverse) works for me. And I think we should have a predicate which is the moral equivalent of Bijective, something like IsEquiv f g, which basically says "they're both ways round".

I really find it such a pain to work with LeftInverse and RightInverse - so at minimum I would like to delete one of these.
In a sense I would rather have a bike shed here - I don't care what shape it is! My bike is getting wet!

How about just Function.IsInverse f g := (f ∘ g = id) because it fits the order of composition, and we forget about left/right? The directions are confusing anyways (#mathlib4 > left and right), even if they're more common when it comes to function inverses
IsInverse is bad because it looks like a true inverse, i.e., inverse on both sides. IsSemiInverse or IsLeftInverse would be fine with me.
Do we have a strong reason to keep HasLeftInverse/HasRightInverse?
One reason to keep LeftInverse is that it does allow for certain dot notation that is otherwise impossible

e.g. consider

/-- A pair of functions form an equivalence when they are mutual two-sided inverses. -/
def IsEquiv (f : α → β) (g : β → α) := RightInverse f g ∧ RightInverse g f

(which I think is a sensible thing we should have in Mathlib at least, as in a sense the lifted form of Bjective).

Clearly you have

protected theorem IsEquiv.rightInverse_left : IsEquiv f g → RightInverse f g := And.left
protected theorem IsEquiv.rightInverse_right {f : α → β} : IsEquiv f g → RightInverse g f := And.right

But also you have 

theorem isEquiv_of_rightInverse_of_leftInverse :
    RightInverse f g → LeftInverse f g → IsEquiv f g := And.intro

protected alias RightInverse.isEquiv_of_leftInverse := isEquiv_of_rightInverse_of_leftInverse
protected alias LeftInverse.isEquiv_of_rightInverse := isEquiv_of_rightInverse_of_leftInverse
And in this case you can't really use dot notation to differentiate between the two. BUT arguably you don't need to (and this is certainly the view we take in many other places).
The Mathlib way would be to have a single IsEquiv.isSemiInverse for one direction, and if you want the other direction you use IsEquiv.symm first.
Yes
I just wanted to acknowledge why you might not want to push LeftInverse into a ditch (I want to push LeftInverse into a ditch).
Isn't it RightInverse we want to kill? And rename LeftInverse to a more neutral thing? (Doesn't really affect your point of course)
I mean they're the same thing aren't they. I suppose you can argue what order the arguments for the predicate should be in.
Yes, the point is that LeftInverse has the "good" order of arguments compared to composition.
Right - sorry I have lost track of which one is good. I think I agree :)
I think what we want is to put the surjective one of the pair first and the injective one second.

I would:

  • ditch HasRightInverse, HasLeftInverse, one of LeftInverse and RightInverse, probably LeftInverse
  • Rename whichever we didn't kill SemiInverse or whatever.
  • Introduce IsEquiv (we've killed three predicates so I don't think inventing a new one is the worse thing, and anywhere where you have both SemiInverse f g and SemiInverse g f you really just want to combine them into one predicate).

I dislike IsLeftInverse because it turns it into a statement about the left argument. IsSemiInverse is better for that reason. Actually I like IsSemiEquiv even better - because it's a predicate on the pair

https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/73342/is-there-a-name-for-a-section-and-a-retraction-together

Evidence that this at least is a non-obvious naming question.
IsSplitPair would be doable. Many exotic colours of bike shed are possible. The bikes are wet.
:) But I think we can get there.
I actually really like IsSplit because it's short.

Wrenna Robson said:

Do we have a strong reason to keep HasLeftInverse/HasRightInverse?

I was about to say "because they're in core", but then I noticed that so are LeftInverse/RightInverse.
Then the renaming discussion is pointless (at least in this channel), and we should just stop using RightInverse and the Has variants, and convert existing theorems.

Yes :) - we are somewhat stuck with it. I don't understand why core upstreamed them, but we did and so here we are. Still - I think usage downstream will affect usage upstream, and in any case, I am a Batteries maintainer and might be minded to upstream sensible approaches...

I think in the first order if Mathlib could deprecate RightInverse and the Has variants that would be good. I don't know that you can literally deprecate RightInverse - can you deprecate an upstream definition on a library basis? - but you see what I mean. That's also a concrete plan of action - that's something somebody could do right now.

@Kim Morrison I would like some advice from you (as a core maintainer) on how to proceed here. The tl;dr is that we feel that LeftInverse and RightInverse should not both exist (and probably it's fine to just keep LeftInverse, though you could consider a rename). We're also not really sure about HasLeftInverse and HasRightInverse. Unfortunately Core has adopted these. Would you be open to their removal/renaming? We're in a difficult situation where honestly I somewhat feel these things being in Core creates a technical debt that is hard for us to repay, because functionally (to me at least) what is in Core is essentially fixed.

I have some other things I'd want to define. To be honest having been doing some refactoring in a personal project recently I'd really like to go at Core's section where it defines even Function.Injective and Function.Surjective and the theorems about them and rationalise and simplify. But I could live with some improvements living in Batteries, for instance. What we can't do is downstream deprecate something upstream.
